newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. Council urges cease-fire in eastern Zaire.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Council urges cease-fire in eastern Zaire.

text.p: Amid bombing raids in eastern Zaire, the U.N. Security Council called on Tuesday for an immediate cease-fire in the central African state as part of a five-point U.N. peace plan.

The council's resolution followed a request from U.N. special envoy Mohammed Sahnoun, who stressed Zaire was more likely to respond to a Security Council demand than one from individual countries or relief agencies, diplomats said.

"There are indications that Zaire will come aboard," said Council President Njuguna Mahugu of Kenya, without elaborating. But Zaire's U.N. envoy, Lukabu Khabouji N'zai, said he did not see how any plan could work unless it was accepted by other nations in the region also.
The 15-member body, by adopting the resolution unanimously, endorsed the plan presented to them in a letter from U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan.
-- the withdrawal of all foreign forces, including mercenaries;
-- respect for the national sovereignty and territorial integrity of Zaire and other states in the region;
-- the protection of refugees and displaced persons;
-- a peaceful settlement of the crisis through dialogue, elections and the convening of an international conference on peace, security and development.
Zaire's ethnic Tutsis took up arms late last year after local authorities tried to expel them to their ancestral homeland in Rwanda.

Foreign mercenaries, notably Serbs, are fighting the rebels alongside Zaire's undisciplined army. Zaire accuses neighboring Rwanda, Burundi and Uganda of backing the rebels. All three deny the charge.

Earlier on Tuesday Zaire announced new bombing raids on rebel-held towns in the east of the country as the foreign ministers of South Africa, Kenya and Tanzania arrived in the capital of Kinshasa for peace talks.

Annan, in his letter to the council, said the foreign ministers of Cameroon, Congo and Zimbabwe were due in Kinshasa shortly along with OAU Secretary-General Salim A. Salim. Sahnoun, who also represents the Organization of Africa Unity, was in Kinshasa too.

He said that Sahnoun's mission would be greatly assisted "if consideration were to be given by the Security Council, on an urgent basis, to an appropriate acknowledgement and support of his initiative."

The war in eastern Zaire is intertwined with the ethnic conflict between Hutus and Tutsis in Rwanda. Hutu hardliners massacred up to 800,000 minority Tutsis and moderate Hutus in 1994 before fleeing en masse into Zaire as a Tutsi-led government seized power in Rwanda.
